_note: What the vacationing psychologists on the Florida beach say about the research (bd kge; dialogue/florida_psychologists.dialogue). Every line they speak carries a tag: [#cite=<id>] names a claim here, verified against its source, whose 'text' is the line's words exactly; [#author=<id>] names a line the author wrote, shipped as he wrote it, as his words, with no source (author_lines); [#interp=<id>] names the psychologists' explanation, the author's rationale with no source (interpretations); [#chat] is their own talk. Sources are only works the author has approved: the site's citations page as it was before 2026-10-27 and his reference list in dev/notebook; he vets every new source first. Self-report data (the author, 2026-10-27: survey and self-report sources are not barred; bring them in to show the disparity with objective data): a claim resting on a survey, self-report, questionnaire or peer nominations carries evidence_kind "self-report" and objective, the id of the record in this file it is set against (an objective_data record: agency data with its source and a .gov url, such as FBI or BJS figures, once he approves them; or a claim that is not self-report), or "none found". objective_data is empty: no self-report claim and no agency figure is in the file today. Claims are not quotes: a claim restates what the source's own text says, and 'evidence' holds that text.

_verification.method: SOP-06 adapted to claims, 2026-10-27: each claim was compared against the cited work's own text, fetched raw (not a model summary): the abstract from NCBI E-utilities (PubMed) or the abstract in the DOI's Crossref record. 'evidence' is the source's sentences, '...' marking a gap between them. Interpretations and the author's own lines are not marked verified: no source states them as worded.
_verification.fields: claims: text, source, url (the DOI), aggregator, collection, population, checked_url, evidence (the source's own sentences), verified, checked_on, note (title when the work is in the author's references rather than on the citations page); for a claim on self-report data, also evidence_kind ("self-report") and objective (an objective_data or claims id, or "none found"). objective_data: id -> {source, url (.gov), and what the figures measure}. author_lines: text, author_words, status. interpretations: text, kind, author_words, note.
_verification.rule: A [#cite] line must be a verified claim from an approved source; a claim on survey or self-report data must carry evidence_kind "self-report" and an objective comparison or "none found"; an [#author] line is the author's words with no source; an [#interp] line is never presented as sourced (tests/test_florida_psychologists.gd).
_verification.removed: 2026-10-27, the author's rule on sources (no source he has not approved, no statistics from surveys): Porsch et al. 2023 and every claim, support and gap record drawn from it; the survey-based claims from Crick & Grotpeter 1995, Garcia-Fernandez et al. 2022 and Hilton et al. 2024 (crick1995_measured with them: it set up crick1995_girls); the author line's support and gap records. Nothing replaces them.

vaillancourt2013_what.text: Indirect aggression includes criticizing a rival's looks, spreading rumors about someone's sex life, and leaving people out.
vaillancourt2013_what.source: Vaillancourt, T. (2013). Do human females use indirect aggression as an intrasexual competition strategy? Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 368(1631), 20130080.
vaillancourt2013_what.population: review of the research on indirect aggression among girls and women
vaillancourt2013_what.evidence: Indirect aggression includes behaviours such as criticizing a competitor's appearance, spreading rumours about a person's sexual behaviour and social exclusion.
vaillancourt2013_what.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 24167310 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

vaillancourt2013_females.text: A 2013 review says women and girls are particularly inclined to indirect aggression, and usually aim it at other women, especially attractive ones.
vaillancourt2013_females.source: Vaillancourt, T. (2013). Do human females use indirect aggression as an intrasexual competition strategy? Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 368(1631), 20130080.
vaillancourt2013_females.population: review of the research on indirect aggression among girls and women
vaillancourt2013_females.evidence: Human females have a particular proclivity for using indirect aggression, which is typically directed at other females, especially attractive and sexually available females, in the context of intrasexual competition for mates.
vaillancourt2013_females.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 24167310 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

vs2011_setup.text: In a 2011 experiment, women saw the same attractive woman dressed either conservatively or in a sexually provocative way.
vs2011_setup.source: Vaillancourt, T., & Sharma, A. (2011). Intolerance of sexy peers: Intrasexual competition among women. Aggressive Behavior, 37(6), 569–577.
vs2011_setup.population: two experiments with women participants; their reactions to a female confederate rated by independent raters blind to condition
vs2011_setup.evidence: Using independent raters, blind to condition, we found that almost all women were rated as reacting negatively ("bitchy") to an attractive female confederate when she was dressed in a sexually provocative manner. In contrast, when she was dressed conservatively, the same confederate was barely noticed by the participants.
vs2011_setup.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 21932332 (NCBI E-utilities raw text; the same abstract is in the Crossref record for the DOI).

vs2011_result.text: Dressed conservatively, she was barely noticed. Dressed provocatively, almost all the women were rated as reacting negatively to her.
vs2011_result.source: Vaillancourt, T., & Sharma, A. (2011). Intolerance of sexy peers: Intrasexual competition among women. Aggressive Behavior, 37(6), 569–577.
vs2011_result.population: two experiments with women participants; their reactions to a female confederate rated by independent raters blind to condition
vs2011_result.evidence: we found that almost all women were rated as reacting negatively ("bitchy") to an attractive female confederate when she was dressed in a sexually provocative manner. In contrast, when she was dressed conservatively, the same confederate was barely noticed by the participants.
vs2011_result.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 21932332 (NCBI E-utilities raw text; the same abstract is in the Crossref record for the DOI).

vs2011_rival.text: In a second study, women didn't want to introduce her to their boyfriends, leave him alone with her, or be friends with her.
vs2011_rival.source: Vaillancourt, T., & Sharma, A. (2011). Intolerance of sexy peers: Intrasexual competition among women. Aggressive Behavior, 37(6), 569–577.
vs2011_rival.population: two experiments with women participants; their reactions to a female confederate rated by independent raters blind to condition
vs2011_rival.evidence: In Study 2, an experimental design was used to assess whether the sexy female confederate from Study 1 was viewed as a sexual rival by women. Results indicated that as hypothesized, women did not want to introduce her to their boyfriend, allow him to spend time alone with her, or be friends with her.
vs2011_rival.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 21932332 (NCBI E-utilities raw text; the same abstract is in the Crossref record for the DOI).

hilton2024_measures.text: The measures and theories of coercive control mostly look at men coercing women.
hilton2024_measures.source: Hilton, N. Z., Ham, E., Radatz, D. L., Smith, C. M., Snow, N., Wintermute, J., Jennings-Fitz-Gerald, E., Lee, J., & Patterson, S. (2024). Coercive control in 2SLGBTQQIA+ relationships: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 25(5), 3713–3728.
hilton2024_measures.population: scoping review of 277 documents (2014 to 2022) on coercive control in 2SLGBTQQIA+ relationships, gray literature included
hilton2024_measures.evidence: Existing measures and theories of intimate partner coercive control largely evaluate men's coercion of women.
hilton2024_measures.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 39066513 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

hilton2024_definition.text: And there's still no agreed definition of coercive control, or an accepted standard for measuring it.
hilton2024_definition.source: Hilton, N. Z., Ham, E., Radatz, D. L., Smith, C. M., Snow, N., Wintermute, J., Jennings-Fitz-Gerald, E., Lee, J., & Patterson, S. (2024). Coercive control in 2SLGBTQQIA+ relationships: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 25(5), 3713–3728.
hilton2024_definition.population: scoping review of 277 documents (2014 to 2022) on coercive control in 2SLGBTQQIA+ relationships, gray literature included
hilton2024_definition.evidence: This review revealed a lack of agreed definition of coercive control or accepted standard of measurement
hilton2024_definition.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 39066513 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

sheppard2017_theory.text: A 2017 theory: people treat conflict between women at work as more of a problem than conflict between men, and that could exaggerate how badly women seem to get along.
sheppard2017_theory.source: Sheppard, L. D., & Aquino, K. (2017). Sisters at arms: A theory of female same-sex conflict and its problematization in organizations. Journal of Management, 43(3), 691–715.
sheppard2017_theory.population: theory paper, no new data: how third parties judge conflict between women and between men at work
sheppard2017_theory.evidence: we set aside consideration of possible gender differences in same-sex conflict frequency and draw from attribution theory to propose that female same-sex conflict is more problematized by third parties than male same-sex conflict, which could produce the exaggerated perception that women have more dysfunctional same-sex workplace relationships than men.
sheppard2017_theory.note: Compared against the article's abstract in the Crossref record for the DOI (raw JSON). A theory paper: the line says what it proposes, not a finding.

benenson2013_harm.text: Women spend their lives providing for their children and grandchildren, so they have to minimize their risk of physical harm.
benenson2013_harm.source: Benenson, J. F. (2013). The development of human female competition: allies and adversaries. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 368(1631), 20130079.
benenson2013_harm.population: review of human female competition from early childhood on
benenson2013_harm.evidence: Throughout their lives, women provide for their own and their children's and grandchildren's needs and thus must minimize their risk of incurring physical harm.
benenson2013_harm.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 24167309 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).
benenson2013_harm.title: The development of human female competition: allies and adversaries

benenson2013_retaliation.text: From early childhood, girls compete in ways that minimize the risk of retaliation.
benenson2013_retaliation.source: Benenson, J. F. (2013). The development of human female competition: allies and adversaries. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 368(1631), 20130079.
benenson2013_retaliation.population: review of human female competition from early childhood on
benenson2013_retaliation.evidence: From early childhood onwards, girls compete using strategies that minimize the risk of retaliation and reduce the strength of other girls.
benenson2013_retaliation.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 24167309 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).
benenson2013_retaliation.title: The development of human female competition: allies and adversaries

stockley2013_lowcost.text: Which fits with indirect aggression being a low-cost, effective way for young women to compete.
stockley2013_lowcost.source: Stockley, P., & Campbell, A. (2013). Female competition and aggression: interdisciplinary perspectives. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 368(1631), 20130073.
stockley2013_lowcost.population: introduction to an interdisciplinary theme issue on female competition and aggression in humans and other vertebrates
stockley2013_lowcost.evidence: Although female aggression takes diverse forms, under most circumstances relatively low-risk competitive strategies are favoured ... coalitions or alliances may reduce risk of retaliation. Consistent with these trends, indirect aggression is a low cost but effective form of competition among young women.
stockley2013_lowcost.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 24167303 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).
stockley2013_lowcost.title: Female competition and aggression: interdisciplinary perspectives

ipv_highest.text: The highest rate of violence is actually between same-sex female couples.
ipv_highest.author_words: Author 2026-10-27, bead persistint-game-kge: his line, as he gave it for the psychologists
ipv_highest.status: The author's line, shipped as he wrote it, as his words. No source: its support and gap records (Porsch et al. 2023, survey data) were removed on 2026-10-27 under his rule on sources.

deterrence_mixed.text: So with a man and a woman, she knows he's stronger, and she keeps it indirect.
